This vignette runs the full `scoranet` workflow on a real dataset and shows
every kind of output it produces: console summaries, result tables, files
written to disk, network plots, and diagnostic figures.

The data are the interferon-beta stimulated PBMCs from Kang et al. (2018),
*Nature Biotechnology* 36, 89-94, distributed as `ifnb` by the
[SeuratData](https://github.com/satijalab/seurat-data) package. Interferon-beta
triggers a strong, well-characterised antiviral response, which makes it a
good test: the workflow should recover interferon signalling in every cell
type.

# Setup


``` r
library(scoranet)
library(Seurat)
library(SeuratData)
library(org.Hs.eg.db)
```


``` r
data("ifnb")
ifnb <- UpdateSeuratObject(ifnb)
ifnb <- NormalizeData(ifnb, verbose = FALSE)

table(ifnb$seurat_annotations, ifnb$stim)[c("CD14 Mono", "CD4 Naive T", "B"), ]
#>              
#>               CTRL STIM
#>   CD14 Mono   2215 2147
#>   CD4 Naive T  978 1526
#>   B            407  571
```

We compare stimulated (`STIM`) against control (`CTRL`) cells in three cell
types. All output files go to a temporary folder. Every function that writes
files takes a directory path with or without a trailing `/`, and creates the
directory if it does not exist.


``` r
cell_types <- c("CD14 Mono", "CD4 Naive T", "B")
out_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "ifnb_results")
```

# 1. Differential expression

`run_cluster_de()` runs `Seurat::FindMarkers()` within each cell type and
prints a short summary per cluster.


``` r
de_results <- run_cluster_de(
  obj         = ifnb,
  clusters    = cell_types,
  cluster_col = "seurat_annotations",
  ident_col   = "stim",
  ident1      = "STIM",
  ident2      = "CTRL"
)
#> i Running DE for "CD14 Mono" (STIM vs CTRL)
#> v Running DE for "CD14 Mono" (STIM vs CTRL) [5.8s]
#> 
#> * Tested genes: 1408
#> * DEGs: 704
#> * Up in STIM: 330
#> * Up in CTRL: 374
#> 
#> i Running DE for "CD4 Naive T" (STIM vs CTRL)
#> v Running DE for "CD4 Naive T" (STIM vs CTRL) [870ms]
#> 
#> * Tested genes: 526
#> * DEGs: 202
#> * Up in STIM: 160
#> * Up in CTRL: 42
#> 
#> i Running DE for "B" (STIM vs CTRL)
#> v Running DE for "B" (STIM vs CTRL) [624ms]
#> 
#> * Tested genes: 812
#> * DEGs: 263
#> * Up in STIM: 187
#> * Up in CTRL: 76
#> 
```

Each cell type returns two tables: `degs` (genes passing the adjusted p-value
and fold-change cutoffs) and `tested` (every gene `FindMarkers` tested).


``` r
names(de_results[["CD14 Mono"]])
#> [1] "degs"   "tested"

c(degs = nrow(de_results[["CD14 Mono"]]$degs),
  tested = nrow(de_results[["CD14 Mono"]]$tested))
#>   degs tested 
#>    704   1408
```


``` r
top_degs <- de_results[["CD14 Mono"]]$degs
top_degs <- top_degs[order(-abs(top_degs$avg_log2FC)), ]
knitr::kable(
  head(top_degs[, c("gene", "avg_log2FC", "pct.1", "pct.2", "p_val_adj", "res")], 10),
  digits = 3, row.names = FALSE
)
```



|gene     | avg_log2FC| pct.1| pct.2| p_val_adj|res                 |
|:--------|----------:|-----:|-----:|---------:|:-------------------|
|CCL8     |      7.068| 0.918| 0.017|         0|Upregulated in STIM |
|CXCL10   |      7.014| 0.984| 0.035|         0|Upregulated in STIM |
|ISG15    |      6.342| 1.000| 0.324|         0|Upregulated in STIM |

The strongest changes are classic interferon-stimulated genes and chemokines
(*CCL8*, *CXCL10*, *ISG15*, and the *IFIT* family), exactly what
interferon-beta should induce. CD14 monocytes respond most strongly: about half of their tested genes
are DEGs.

`write_de()` saves both tables per cell type:


``` r
write_de(de_results, outSubDir = file.path(out_dir, "DE"))
list.files(file.path(out_dir, "DE"))
#> [1] "B_DE_Results.csv"             "B_tested_genes.csv"          
#> [3] "CD14_Mono_DE_Results.csv"     "CD14_Mono_tested_genes.csv"  
#> [5] "CD4_Naive_T_DE_Results.csv"   "CD4_Naive_T_tested_genes.csv"
```

# 2. GO over-representation analysis

`run_go_ora()` runs `clusterProfiler::enrichGO()` on each cell type's DEGs.
Here each cell type's tested genes are used as its background
(`use_tested_universe = TRUE`), because genes that were never tested could not
have been DEGs.


``` r
go_results <- run_go_ora(
  de_list             = de_results,
  org_db              = org.Hs.eg.db,
  use_tested_universe = TRUE,
  ont                 = "BP",
  outputDir           = file.path(out_dir, "ORA")
)
#> 
#> 
#> -- GO set: CD14 Mono --
#> 
#> Genesets tested: 2846
#> After filtering: 44
#> Retention proportion: 0.015
#> 
#> -- GO set: CD4 Naive T --
#> 
#> Genesets tested: 1520
#> After filtering: 65
#> Retention proportion: 0.043
#> 
#> -- GO set: B --
#> 
#> Genesets tested: 1940
#> After filtering: 90
#> Retention proportion: 0.046
```

Each element is a standard `clusterProfiler` `enrichResult`:


``` r
go_cd14 <- as.data.frame(go_results[["CD14 Mono"]])
knitr::kable(
  head(go_cd14[, c("Description", "GeneRatio", "BgRatio", "p.adjust", "Count")], 10),
  digits = 8, row.names = FALSE
)
```



|Description                                                               |GeneRatio |BgRatio  |   p.adjust| Count|

The top terms are antiviral and cytokine responses.

A QC summary of how many gene sets were tested and retained is attached to the
result as its `"qc"` attribute, and saved as `GO_ORA_QC_summary.csv` when
`outputDir` is given. `outputDir` is optional: leave it as `NULL` to keep
everything in R.


``` r
knitr::kable(attr(go_results, "qc"), row.names = FALSE)
```



|set         | tested| retained|  prop|
|:-----------|------:|--------:|-----:|
|CD14 Mono   |   2846|       44| 0.015|
|CD4 Naive T |   1520|       65| 0.043|
|B           |   1940|       90| 0.046|



CD14 monocytes have the most DEGs but the fewest enriched terms. With the
tested-gene background, half of their background genes are DEGs, so a term
needs a very large share of DEGs to stand out. This is the tested-gene
universe being appropriately conservative, not a lack of signal.

`write_go()` saves the results, adding numeric gene-ratio columns:


``` r
write_go(go_results, outSubDir = file.path(out_dir, "ORA"))
list.files(file.path(out_dir, "ORA"))
#> [1] "B_GO_ORA_Results.csv"           "CD14_Mono_GO_ORA_Results.csv"  
#> [3] "CD4_Naive_T_GO_ORA_Results.csv" "GO_ORA_QC_summary.csv"
```

# 3. Choosing network settings

Before building the final networks, the diagnostics show how the overlap
threshold and Leiden resolution shape them. A first pass at the default
settings is enough to run them (the console summary is hidden here).


``` r
net_default <- run_comparison_networks(
  go_list     = go_results,
  de_list     = de_results,
  comp_label  = "STIM_vs_CTRL",
  base_outdir = file.path(out_dir, "default")
)

dx_default <- run_network_diagnostics(net_default, de_results, go_results)
```

## Overlap threshold

Two GO terms are connected when the Jaccard overlap of their DE genes is at
least `overlap_threshold`; terms with no connection are dropped.


``` r
dx_default$networks[["CD14 Mono"]]$overlap_threshold
```

<div class="figure">
<img src="figures/ifnb-diag-threshold-1.png" alt="plot of chunk diag-threshold" width="100%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk diag-threshold</p>
</div>

Almost every pair of enriched terms shares at least one gene, and many share
only a few. Raising the threshold from the default 0.1 to 0.2 roughly halves
the number of edges while dropping only two terms, so we use 0.2. See
`DIAGNOSTICS.md` in the package repository for a full guide to reading these
figures.

# 4. Pathway overlap networks

We rebuild the networks with the chosen threshold.


``` r
net_results <- run_comparison_networks(
  go_list           = go_results,
  de_list           = de_results,
  comp_label        = "STIM_vs_CTRL",
  base_outdir       = out_dir,
  overlap_threshold = 0.2,
  leiden_resolution = 1,
  theme_min_terms   = 2
)
names(net_results)
#> [1] "CD14 Mono"   "CD4 Naive T" "B"
```

## Leiden resolution

With the threshold settled, the resolution sweep checks the clustering:


``` r
dx <- run_network_diagnostics(net_results, de_results, go_results)
dx$networks[["CD14 Mono"]]$leiden_sweep
```

<div class="figure">
<img src="figures/ifnb-diag-sweep-1.png" alt="plot of chunk diag-sweep" width="100%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk diag-sweep</p>
</div>

A good resolution sits on a plateau where the cluster count is steady,
modularity is high, and stability (agreement between random seeds, measured as
the adjusted Rand index) is close to 1. Section 7 defines each metric.
Here the default resolution of 1 sits at the modularity peak with perfect
stability, so we keep it. Modularity is modest because nearly every term in
this network is part of one connected interferon response.

If the sweep pointed to a different resolution, `recluster_network()` would
re-run Leiden on the existing network without rebuilding it, keeping the node
layout so plots before and after are directly comparable:


``` r
net_fine <- recluster_network(net_results[["CD14 Mono"]], resolution = 1.5)
net_fine$cluster_stats
#>   cluster avg_degree n_terms
#> 1       1   30.50000       2
#> 2       2   20.85714       7
#> 3       3   20.50000       4
#> 4       4   25.66667       3
#> 5       5    1.00000       2
#> 6       6   13.35714      14
#> 7       7   10.33333       3
#> 8       8   16.28571       7
```

Each network result holds the `igraph` object, tables of terms and clusters,
the settings used, and the node layout. `plot_network()` draws it as one of
four editable `ggplot` objects: `regulation`, `leiden`, `zscore` or `themes`.


``` r
net <- net_results[["CD14 Mono"]]
net
#> <scoranet_network> STIM_vs_CTRL_CD14_Mono
#>   Nodes: 42  Edges: 350  Clusters: 4
#>   Leiden resolution: 1 (modularity)  Overlap threshold: 0.2
#>   Plot with plot_network(); tables with network_tables().
names(net)
#>  [1] "network"            "clustering"         "overlap_matrix"     "go_term_df"        
#>  [5] "cluster_stats"      "leiden_resolution"  "objective_function" "overlap_threshold" 
#>  [9] "seed"               "term_genes"         "cluster_themes"     "cluster_palette"   
#> [13] "layout"             "collection_name"    "ident1"             "ident2"            
#> [17] "file_stem"          "theme_args"
```

## Direction

Nodes are GO terms, coloured by whether their DE genes go up in `STIM` (red),
up in `CTRL` (blue), or both (grey, "mixed"). Edge width shows overlap; node
size shows the number of DE genes in the term. Almost the whole network is
red: stimulation switches on the antiviral program.


``` r
plot_network(net, "regulation")
```

<p class="caption">plot of chunk plot-regulation</p>
</div>

The `zscore` plot shows how strongly each term leans one way, on a continuous
scale. The darkest red terms are the core defence and innate immune terms of
the interferon response. The four blue terms, up in `CTRL`, form the two small
clusters (translation and the broad proliferation terms); one pale term in the
immune cluster is mixed, with about as many genes going up as down.



## Cluster themes

The `themes` plot outlines each Leiden cluster and labels it with the GO terms
its members fall under in the GO hierarchy, with how many of the cluster's
terms they cover. The two large clusters separate the direct antiviral
response (viral process, response to type I interferon) from the broader
innate immune response. Of the two small clusters, translation is clearly down
in `STIM`. The other holds two broad "regulation of cell population
proliferation" terms; it leans only weakly down and is built from cytokine,
chemokine and matrix genes that carry proliferation annotations (see the driver
genes below), so it is better read as an annotation catch-all than as a change
in proliferation.


``` r
plot_network(net, "themes", min_terms = 2)
```

# 5. Interpreting modules

## Driver genes

Which genes is each cluster built on? A gene's share is the fraction of the
cluster's terms that contain it (defined in Section 7).


``` r
dx$networks[["CD14 Mono"]]$driver_genes
```

<div class="figure">
<img src="figures/ifnb-diag-drivers-1.png" alt="plot of chunk diag-drivers" width="100%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk diag-drivers</p>
</div>

The antiviral cluster is built on the *OAS* and *IFITM* families. The innate
immune cluster shares *OAS1* and *OAS3* and adds *GBP5* and *CASP1*, all up in
`STIM`. *IL1B* also runs through most of its terms but goes **down** (log2FC
about -2.7): type I interferon is known to suppress IL-1β production
(Guarda et al. 2011, *Immunity*), so this module is an interferon-driven
innate response, not an IL-1β-driven one. The translation cluster is built on
ribosomal protein genes that go down after stimulation, and the small
"proliferation" cluster on *CXCL10*, *TNFSF13B* and *CD38* (up) with *IL1B* and
*VCAN* (down).

# 6. Splitting by direction

With `split_direction = TRUE`, ORA runs separately on up- and down-regulated
genes, and a network is built for each direction. Each test is then made
against fewer, more coherent genes, which helps in two cases: when one
direction has far fewer DEGs and would be drowned out by the other, and, as
here, when DEGs make up a large share of the background (half of the tested
genes in CD14 monocytes, see Section 2), which dilutes a combined test. Every
module in a split network also has a single direction.


``` r
go_split <- run_go_ora(
  de_list             = de_results["CD14 Mono"],
  org_db              = org.Hs.eg.db,
  use_tested_universe = TRUE,
  split_direction     = TRUE,
  outputDir           = file.path(out_dir, "ORA_split")
)

net_split <- run_comparison_networks(
  go_list           = go_split,
  de_list           = de_results,
  comp_label        = "STIM_vs_CTRL_split",
  base_outdir       = out_dir,
  overlap_threshold = 0.2,
  split_direction   = TRUE
)
names(net_split)
#> [1] "CD14 Mono_up"   "CD14 Mono_down"
```


``` r
plot_network(net_split[["CD14 Mono_up"]], "themes")
```

<div class="figure">
<img src="figures/ifnb-split-up-1.png" alt="plot of chunk split-up" width="100%" />
<p class="caption">plot of chunk split-up</p>
</div>

Built from the up-regulated genes alone, the CD14 monocyte response resolves
into many distinct modules: type I interferon production, interleukin-1
production, chemokine response and leukocyte chemotaxis, adaptive immune
activation, and more. Most of these terms were not enriched in the combined
analysis at all: it found 44
enriched terms, while the up-regulated genes alone give
178. The interleukin-1 production module reflects regulators of IL-1 that go
up (such as *GBP5* and *CASP1*), not *IL1B* itself, which goes down.

The down-regulated genes give a much smaller network of
5 terms (translation and
ribosome biogenesis), the same signal as the translation cluster in the
combined network.

# 7. Reading the results

This section defines every quantity the workflow reports and every column in
the files it writes.

## How the network is built

**Jaccard overlap.** Each GO term is represented by its DE genes: the genes
annotated to the term that are also in the DEG list. For two terms with DE gene
sets $A$ and $B$, the Jaccard overlap is

$$J(A, B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|},$$

the number of DE genes the terms share divided by the number of DE genes in
either. It runs from 0 (no shared genes) to 1 (identical gene sets). For
example, a term with DE genes {*ISG15*, *IFIT1*, *IFIT3*, *MX1*} and one with
{*IFIT1*, *IFIT3*, *OAS1*} share 2 of 5 distinct genes, so $J = 0.4$.

**Edges.** Two terms are connected when $J \ge$ `overlap_threshold` (0.2
here), and the edge width shows $J$. Terms with no edge at that threshold are
**isolates** and are dropped from the network.

**Node size** grows with the number of DE genes in the term (on a log scale).

**Degree** is the number of other terms a term is connected to. High-degree
terms are hubs: their genes overlap with many other terms, which is typical of
broad parent terms such as "immune response".

## Direction

For each term, using only its DE genes:

- `n_up` and `n_down` are the numbers of genes with positive and negative
  log2 fold change (up in `STIM` and up in `CTRL` here).
- `avg_log2FC` and `median_log2FC` are the mean and median log2 fold change.
  The median is less affected by one gene with an extreme fold change.
- The **direction z-score** is
  $$z = \frac{n_{up} - n_{down}}{\sqrt{n_{up} + n_{down}}}.$$
  It combines how consistently the genes move with how many genes support it:
  9 up and 1 down gives $z = 2.5$; 3 up and 2 down gives $z = 0.45$; a single
  up gene gives $z = 1$.
- `regulation` calls a term `up` when $z \ge$ `zscore_threshold` (default 1),
  `down` when $z \le -$`zscore_threshold`, and `mixed` otherwise.

This direction z-score is not the same as the `zScore` column that
`clusterProfiler` adds to the ORA results, which measures enrichment, not
direction (see below).

## Clustering

**Leiden clustering** groups terms that are more densely connected to each
other than to the rest of the network. Edge weights ($J$) are used, so
strongly overlapping terms pull harder.

**Resolution** sets how finely the network is split: higher values give more,
smaller clusters.

**Modularity** scores how well a partition separates the network. It is the
share of edge weight that falls within clusters, minus the share expected if
edges were placed at random while keeping each term's total edge weight. Values
near 0 mean no better than random; values above about 0.3 indicate clear
structure. The sweep always reports standard modularity (resolution 1), so it
can be compared across resolutions.

**Adjusted Rand index (ARI)** measures how well two partitions of the same
terms agree. It counts pairs of terms that both partitions put together, or
both keep apart, and corrects for the agreement expected by chance. It is 1
when the partitions are identical and about 0 when they agree no more than
random partitions would. **Stability** in the sweep is the mean ARI over every
pair of random seeds at a resolution. A value of 1 means the clustering does
not depend on the seed.

## Cluster themes and the ratios on the network

Each cluster is labelled with up to two GO terms that its terms fall under in
the GO hierarchy (its "ancestors"). A label such as

> viral process / response to type I interferon (12/16)

means that 12 of the cluster's 16 terms are one of these ancestors or a
descendant of one. An ancestor is only used if it covers at least
`theme_ancestor_min_share` of the cluster (default 15%) and has at most
`theme_ancestor_max_size` descendant terms (default 1,000, to exclude very
generic terms). Among those, ancestors are picked one at a time to cover as
many still-uncovered terms as possible, weighted by how specific they are.
When no ancestor qualifies, the label falls back to the hub term and says
"(hub; no shared GO parent)", which often means the cluster mixes unrelated
terms.

The other label styles (`label_by` in `plot_network()`) are:

- `keywords`: the most distinctive words in the cluster's term names,
  down-weighting words common to all clusters.
- `phrase`: the top term name, after merging near-identical names.
- `hub`: the cluster's highest-degree term.

## Driver genes

For each cluster $c$ with $N_c$ terms, a gene's **share** is

$$\text{share}(g, c) = \frac{n_{terms}(g, c)}{N_c},$$

where $n_{terms}(g, c)$ is the number of the cluster's terms whose DE genes
include $g$. The genes with the highest $n_{terms}$ are the cluster's drivers
(ties are broken by larger $|\log_2 FC|$). Dot colour is the gene's log2 fold
change, and dot size spans the range of shares shown, so read exact values
from the legend.

A high share means a gene is annotated to most of the cluster's terms, so the
cluster's theme rests on it. It does not mean the gene is specific to that
cluster: broadly annotated genes such as *IL1B* can drive several clusters,
and in a two-term cluster every shared gene has a share of 100%.

## Output files

### Differential expression (`DE/`)

`<cell type>_DE_Results.csv` holds the DEGs and `<cell type>_tested_genes.csv`
every gene `FindMarkers()` tested. Columns:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `p_val` | Unadjusted p-value (Wilcoxon rank-sum test by default) |
| `avg_log2FC` | log2 fold change of mean expression, `ident1` vs `ident2`; positive = higher in `ident1` |
| `pct.1`, `pct.2` | Fraction of cells expressing the gene in `ident1` and `ident2` |
| `p_val_adj` | Bonferroni-adjusted p-value (over all genes in the dataset) |
| `gene`, `cluster`, `comparison` | Gene symbol, cell type, and `"<ident1>_vs_<ident2>"` |
| `res` | DEGs only: `"Upregulated in <ident1>"` or `"Upregulated in <ident2>"` |

A gene is a DEG when `p_val_adj` $\le$ `padj_thresh` (0.05) and
$|$`avg_log2FC`$| >$ `logfc_thresh` (0.5).

### GO over-representation (`ORA/`)

`<cell type>_GO_ORA_Results.csv` holds one row per enriched GO term:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ID`, `Description` | GO ID and term name |
| `GeneRatio` | $k/n$: DEGs in the term / DEGs annotated to any tested GO term |
| `BgRatio` | $M/N$: background genes in the term / background genes annotated to any tested GO term |
| `RichFactor` | $k/M$: the fraction of the term's background genes that are DEGs |
| `FoldEnrichment` | $(k/n) / (M/N)$: how many times more often the term appears among DEGs than in the background |
| `zScore` | Enrichment z-score from `clusterProfiler`: how far $k$ is above the count expected by chance, in standard deviations. Not the direction z-score |
| `pvalue` | One-sided hypergeometric test p-value |
| `p.adjust` | Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value; terms with `p.adjust` < 0.05 enter the network |
| `qvalue` | Storey q-value |
| `geneID` | The term's DEGs, separated by `/` |
| `Count` | $k$, the number of DEGs in the term |
| `geneRatio_num`, `geneRatio_den` | $k$ and $n$ as numbers, added by `write_go()` |

The background is every gene tested in the cell type when
`use_tested_universe = TRUE`. Only GO terms with 5 to 300 annotated
background genes are tested. `GO_ORA_QC_summary.csv` (written when
`run_go_ora()` is given an `outputDir`, and always available in R as
`attr(go_results, "qc")`) lists, for each cell type, how many GO terms were `tested`, how many were `retained` as
significant, and the proportion (`prop`); with `simplify = TRUE` it adds
`after_simplify`, the count left after redundant terms are merged.

### Networks (`<comparison>/networks/`)

| File | One row per | Columns |
|---|---|---|
| `<cell type>_network_summary.csv` | metric | `nodes`, `edges` and `clusters` counts |
| `<cell type>-cluster-stats.csv` | cluster | `cluster`; `avg_degree`, the mean degree of its terms (how densely connected it is); `n_terms` |
| `<cell type>-cluster-membership.csv` | GO term | `go_term`, `cluster`, `degree`, `regulation`, `avg_log2FC`, `median_log2FC`, `n_up`, `n_down`, `zscore` (direction), `go_id`, `leiden_resolution`, and `genes` (the term's DE genes, separated by `/`). Sorted by cluster, then degree |
| `<cell type>-cluster-themes.csv` | cluster | `cluster`, `n_terms`, `ancestor` (names joined by ` / `), `ancestor_id`, `ancestor_n_covered` (the numerator in the plot labels), `keywords`, `phrase`, `hub` |

`network_tables(net)` returns the same four tables in R. The PNG files are the
four `plot_network()` types: `-regulation`, `-clustered-leiden`, `-zscore` and
`-themes`.
